Why This Is Not a 2008 Replay
1. The Core Problem Is Inflation & Valuation, Not Systemic Insolvency
In 2008, the crisis was triggered by excessive leverage in subprime mortgage derivatives, causing major banks (like Lehman Brothers) to fail and credit markets to lock up. Today, corporate and bank balance sheets are well-capitalized, and global economic growth remains on solid footing. The current friction comes from sticky inflation (~3.7% in the US) and a valuation reset in mega-cap AI stocks—closer in character to the 2000 tech valuation reset or 1970s/2022 supply-driven inflation cycles than 2008.  
2. Central Banks Are Fighting Heat, Not Deflation
In 2008, policymakers were terrified of a deflationary depression and were flooding the system with cheap money. In late 2026, the Federal Reserve, ECB, and Bank of England are keeping interest rates elevated—and even weighing further 25 bps hikes—precisely because consumer demand and labor markets are strong enough to sustain higher rates while energy shocks keep prices sticky.

Oil is priced around geopolitical risk premia in the Middle East rather than runaway speculative demand, and rising US/global output is keeping a lid on prices.
